summary: Extends IS-IS so any cryptographic authentication algorithm can be used, in addition to the plain-text and HMAC-MD5 schemes already defined. This lets operators choose stronger or newer algorithms, such as the SHA family, without changing the protocol again. It is on the standards track and has been updated by later documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of being locked into one kind of secret stamp for routing messages, routers can now pick from many. If one stamp is found weak, they can switch to another.

subtitle: A generic IS-IS authentication type that lets routers protect their messages with HMAC and the SHA family of hashes.

tldr.problem: IS-IS only had cleartext passwords and HMAC-MD5 for authenticating its messages, and there were concerns about the ultimate strength of MD5.
tldr.mechanism: A new authentication type, CRYPTO_AUTH (type 3) in TLV 10, carries a 2-octet Key ID that selects a security association and an HMAC result computed with SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512.
tldr.outcome: Operators can switch hash algorithms and keys without disrupting adjacencies. The scheme gives no confidentiality and no replay protection. RFC 6232 and RFC 6233 update it.

today: RFC 5310 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2009. It has been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why Generic Authentication
sections.content:
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) can authenticate its Protocol Data Units (PDUs) with an authentication TLV, number 10. The first octet of its value says which type is used: type 0 is reserved, type 1 is a cleartext password, type 54 is HMAC-MD5 (added by RFC 5304), and type 255 is for routing domain private methods.

This RFC adds a new type, CRYPTO_AUTH, that can name any authentication algorithm, and explains how to use HMAC with SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512. The authors say that, although no openly published attacks on HMAC-MD5 existed at the time, some reports raised concern about the strength of MD5. They also propose dropping per-interface keys in favour of Key IDs that map to security associations.

The mechanism gives no confidentiality, because PDUs are sent in the clear. The RFC argues that a routing protocol advertises topology and normally does not need secrecy.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers send each other messages and sign them so nobody can fake them. This lets them choose from several kinds of signature instead of just one.

sections.title: The IS-IS Security Association
sections.content:
An IS-IS Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters shared by two legitimate IS-IS speakers. It has three parts.

  • Key ID: a two-octet unsigned integer, configured by the operator, that identifies the SA. The receiver finds the active SA from the Key ID in the incoming PDU. If several SAs are valid for an outbound interface, the sender may use any of them.
  • Authentication Algorithm: HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 or HMAC-SHA-512. It is never sent on the wire, so each implementation picks its own internal representation.
  • Authentication Key: the secret, whose length is variable and depends on the algorithm.

Because each Key ID names both an algorithm and a key, an operator can change keys, or even algorithms, without disrupting an IS-IS peering. Key chains with fixed lifetimes are suggested, but how they work is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each secret comes with a label number. The label tells the receiver which secret and which stamp style to check with, without saying them out loud.

sections.title: The Authentication TLV
sections.content:
A new authentication code, 3, marks CRYPTO_AUTH. It goes in the first octet of the existing authentication TLV (type 10). After the Type, Length and Auth Type octets come the two-octet Key ID and then the variable-length authentication data.

The data length matches the hash output size, so larger hashes make PDUs bigger on the wire. The TLV length is 23 for HMAC-SHA-1, 31 for HMAC-SHA-224, 35 for HMAC-SHA-256, 51 for HMAC-SHA-384 and 67 for HMAC-SHA-512. These figures include two octets for the Key ID and one for the authentication type.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature goes in a labelled box inside each message. A bigger stamp makes the box, and so the message, a bit bigger.

sections.title: How the HMAC Is Computed
sections.content:
The computation follows FIPS 198. The block size B is 64 for SHA-1 and SHA-256, and 128 for SHA-384 and SHA-512. L is the hash length in octets. Opad is 0x5c repeated B times, Ipad is 0x36 repeated B times, and Apad is 0x878FE1F3 repeated L/4 times.

  1. Key preparation: the key Ko is always L octets. A key of exactly L octets is used as is, a longer key is replaced by H(K), and a shorter key is padded with zeros at the end.
  2. First hash: the Authentication Data field is filled with Apad and the Authentication Type is set to 0x3. Then First-Hash = H(Ko XOR Ipad || (IS-IS PDU)).
  3. Second hash: Second-Hash = H(Ko XOR Opad || First-Hash).
  4. Result: the second hash is the authentication data, and its length always equals the digest size of H.
sections.plainLanguage: The router mixes the secret with the message, scrambles it, mixes the secret in again, and scrambles it a second time. The final result is the signature.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
Sending: the router picks the active key's SA. If there is no active key, the PDU is discarded. It fills the authentication type, length and Key ID, sets the Checksum and Remaining Lifetime fields of Link State Packets to zero, computes the data and places it after the Key ID. Sequence Number PDUs use the area authentication string at Level 1 and the domain string at Level 2. IIH (Hello) PDUs use the link level string, and their data MUST be computed after padding to the MTU size unless padding is disabled. Implementations MUST NOT include the Checksum TLV in Sequence Number or Hello PDUs.

Receiving: the SA is found from the Key ID. The router saves the Authentication Value, Checksum and Remaining Lifetime fields, sets the first to Apad and the others to zero, recomputes the data and compares. If it does not match, the PDU is discarded and an error event SHOULD be logged.

An implementation MAY offer a transition mode where it sends CRYPTO_AUTH data but does not verify it, as a migration aid.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender stamps each message and the receiver stamps its own copy the same way. If the stamps differ, the message is thrown away.

sections.title: Limits and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says openly that the mechanism is not perfect. It raises the work an attacker must do without making deployment too complex. It confirms the PDU came from a system with access to the area or domain password, rather than identifying the specific originator.

  • No replay protection: old IIHs could be replayed to bring down an adjacency, and old CSNPs and PSNPs could cause a flood of LSPs. Cryptographic sequence numbers are mentioned as an option but left out of scope.
  • Remaining Lifetime is not authenticated, so intermediate systems can age LSPs without recomputing the data. An attacker could exploit this.
  • Transition mode leaves a router vulnerable, so it should be used only while migrating.

Keys should be changed periodically, implementations MUST be able to store and use more than one key at once, and keys must never be sent in cleartext. Full digital signatures were considered and rejected because of their computational burden.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp proves a message came from someone who knows the secret, but a bad guy could still replay an old stamped message, so it is not perfect.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered the value 3 for Cryptographic Authentication (CRYPTO_AUTH) in the "IS-IS Authentication Type Codes for TLV 10" subregistry that RFC 5304 established.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of stamp types got a new entry, number 3, for this one.
